about: What the streets say: the tombs' epitaphs, the shops' signs, the crossroads shrines age by age, the streets' paving and the corner names (tools/make_rome_streets.py).

epitaphs.text: TO THE SPIRITS OF THE DEAD. GAIUS VETTIUS, FREEDMAN OF GAIUS, BAKER, LIVED 61 YEARS. ANTONIA HIS WIFE MADE THIS FOR HIM AND FOR HERSELF WHILE SHE LIVED.
epitaphs.note: A freedman's tomb: the trade named with pride, the wife's name after. D M at the top, to the spirits of the dead, on nearly every stone from the emperors on.

epitaphs.text: STOP, TRAVELLER, AND LOOK TO YOUR LEFT. I WAS A CHILD OF NINE YEARS, THREE MONTHS AND FOUR DAYS. MY FATHER AND MOTHER SET THIS UP AND WEEP.
epitaphs.note: The Romans counted the days of a child's life on its stone. Half of all children died before ten, and the roads out of every city are lined with them.

epitaphs.text: I WAS NOT. I WAS. I AM NOT. I DO NOT CARE.
epitaphs.note: Non fui, fui, non sum, non curo: the Epicurean's epitaph, cut on hundreds of stones, sometimes shortened to its initials, N F F N S N C.

epitaphs.text: HERE LIES TITUS FLAVIUS HERMES, SOLDIER OF THE TENTH URBAN COHORT, SERVED 18 YEARS, LIVED 40. HIS HEIR SET THIS UP AS HE WISHED.
epitaphs.note: A soldier's stone gives his unit and his years of service before his years of life. His heir, not his family: soldiers could not marry while they served.

epitaphs.text: BATHS, WINE AND LOVE RUIN OUR BODIES, BUT BATHS, WINE AND LOVE MAKE LIFE.
epitaphs.note: Balnea vina Venus corrumpunt corpora nostra, sed vitam faciunt: a joke for the road, on the tomb of a man who evidently had all three.

epitaphs.text: TO AULUS GRANIUS, AUCTIONEER, A MAN OF CONSEQUENCE, WORTHY AND TRUSTED. HE WHO WAS SHOUTING FROM THE PLATFORM IS SILENT NOW. FAREWELL.
epitaphs.note: An auctioneer's, on the road: his trade was to shout, and his stone says so. The dead speak, the passer-by answers: farewell.

epitaphs.text: MAY THE EARTH LIE LIGHT ON YOU. HERE RESTS CLAUDIA PRIMA, AGED 27. SHE WORKED THE WOOL, SHE KEPT THE HOUSE, SHE WAS CHASTE, SHE WAS MERRY.
epitaphs.note: Sit tibi terra levis, S T T L: may the earth lie light. The wife's virtues are the same on every stone for four centuries: wool, the house, chastity, and once in a while, merry.

epitaphs.text: THIS TOMB IS NOT TO PASS TO THE HEIR. WHOEVER DEFILES IT SHALL PAY TWENTY THOUSAND SESTERCES TO THE TREASURY OF THE VESTALS.
epitaphs.note: H M H N S: hoc monumentum heredem non sequitur. A tomb was property, and the dead protected it with a fine, since no one else would.

epitaphs.text: GAIUS, FLUTE-PLAYER, PLAYED FOR THE SACRIFICES ON THE CAPITOL. HE LIES HERE. HIS FRIENDS OF THE GUILD OF FLUTE-PLAYERS MADE THIS.
epitaphs.note: A guild's stone: the poor were buried by their clubs, which met once a month for dinner and once for each funeral. The flute-players' guild was as old as the kings.

epitaphs.text: IN PEACE. AURELIA, WHO LIVED 34 YEARS, A CHRISTIAN, SLEEPS HERE. SHE DEPOSITED ON THE THIRD DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF MAY. IN THE LORD.
epitaphs.note: The Christian stone: no D M, no office, no years counted from birth but the day of burial, the day she was born to the other life, and the dead 'sleeping'.

epitaphs.text: I, WHO LIE HERE, WAS ONCE WHAT YOU ARE. YOU WHO READ WILL BE WHAT I AM.
epitaphs.note: The stone speaks to whoever reads it, and there is no answer. Every road out of Rome says it a hundred times before the second milestone.

heroic.note: A shrine of the Lares of the crossing (the Lares Compitales): two dancing youths painted on the wall of a little aedicula, a snake below them for the spirit of the place, an altar in front, a garland fresh every morning. The Compitalia in January is their festival, and the whole street eats together.

early.note: The Lares of the crossing in their aedicula, the garland of the day on it, a pinch of meal on the altar. Each crossing has its own, kept by the people of its street, slaves and freedmen among them; the magistrate of the street sees to its games.

republic.note: The Lares of the crossing. The Senate banned the street clubs that kept them in 64 BC and Clodius brought them back in 58 as his gangs; the shrine is a party headquarters now, its games a riot.

empire.note: The Lares of the crossing, with the Emperor's Genius between them since Augustus, who divided the city into 265 wards each with its shrine and its four freedmen masters. The masters wear the toga praetexta one day a year and are prouder of it than of anything.

late.note: A niche where the Lares were: the two youths painted over, a cross scratched in the plaster, and someone's lamp. The street still keeps it; it is not sure of whom.

collapse.note: The niche is broken and the altar's top knocked off. Someone has put a jar of flowers in the rubble all the same.

fall.note: A block of travertine at a crossing, a hollow in its top worn by four centuries of small offerings. Nobody knows what it was.

corners.note: The Romans put no names on their streets: you asked. The painted names on the corner shops are for you, in the letters the shops' notices used.

gates.Capene Gate: The Servian wall's gate to the Appian Way, where the road south leaves the city: tufa, from the wall built after the Gauls in 378 BC, ten metres high and four thick, a tower each side, and an aqueduct dripping over it since the Marcia was built, so that Juvenal calls it the wet gate. The tombs begin outside it.
gates.Esquiline Gate: The gate on the city's east side, where the agger, the great earth rampart behind the wall, is highest: a hundred feet thick with a ditch in front. The Gauls, Hannibal, the slave armies were all expected here; the executioners' ground and the paupers' pits lie outside it.
gates.Carmental Gate: The gate under the Capitol toward the river, named for Carmenta, Evander's mother. The three hundred and six Fabii marched out of its right-hand arch to die at the Cremera, and no one uses that arch since.
gates.Trigemina Gate: The triple gate to the river port and the road to Ostia, under the Aventine: the busiest of them all, the carts of grain and oil going in and out of the Emporium.
gates.Colline Gate: The gate at the north end of the Quirinal, where the Salarian Way leaves: Hannibal rode up to it in 211 BC and looked at the walls, and Sulla fought the Samnites under it in 82 BC and won Rome.
gates.Fontinal Gate: The gate of the springs, on the Capitol's north side toward the Campus, where the Via Lata goes out to the Flaminian Way.
gates.Caelimontane Gate: The gate on the Caelian toward the Latin Way. Under the emperors the wall is a line of stones through people's yards here, and the gate an arch in a street.
gates.Naevian Gate: The gate through the Aventine's back toward the Ardeatine Way and the sheep pastures south of the city.
gates.Raudusculan Gate: The bronze-sheathed gate at the Aventine's foot, said to be named for the raw bronze (raudus) on its doors, or for a general's horns.
gates.Lavernal Gate: The gate of Laverna, the goddess of thieves, on the Aventine's west side, with her grove and altar beside it.
gates.Flumentan Gate: The river gate, low on the bank below the Capitol, where the Tiber floods in first.
gates.Sanqual Gate: The gate of Sancus, the Sabine god of oaths, on the Quirinal's south side.
gates.Salutary Gate: The gate by the Temple of Salus on the Quirinal's brow.
gates.Quirinal Gate: The gate at the Quirinal's north, where the road to the Sabine country climbs out.
gates.Viminal Gate: The gate in the agger between the Viminal and the Esquiline, the wall at its strongest.
gates.Querquetulan Gate: The oak-grove gate, between the Esquiline and the Caelian, named for the grove that stood here before the city reached it.
